q: 1. Reconnaissance survey means .........
options: conducting the surveys to get the plan of the site
conducting the surveys to get contours of the site
visual inspection of the site and study of the topographical features
explain: Reconnaissance is the preliminary inspection of a site to gather information about its topography, accessibility, and general characteristics before detailed surveying begins.

q: 2. The safety of the structure can be disturbed by ...........
options: lowering or rising of water table
excavations in the immediate vicinity of the structure
mining or tunneling operations in the neighborhood
explain: Structural stability depends on the ground conditions; changes in water pressure, nearby soil removal (excavation), or underground voids (mining) can all cause settlement or failure.

q: 3. The investigation method suitable for shallow depths is .........
explain: Open excavation (trial pits) is the most direct and economical way to inspect soil strata at shallow depths, allowing for visual inspection of the soil layers.

q: 4. The weight and fall used in standard penetrometer test to drive the cone are .......
explain: The Standard Penetration Test (SPT) uses a standard weight of 65 kg (often cited as 63.5 kg in some codes) falling from a height of 75 cm.

q: 5. The soil investigation method using the penetrometers belongs to the category of .......
explain: Penetrometer tests (like SPT or CPT) are classified as sub-surface soundings because they measure the resistance of soil to the penetration of a sampler or cone.

q: 6. The number of blows recorded in a standard penetration test is for a penetration of .......
explain: The 'N' value in an SPT test is the number of blows required to drive the sampler for the last 30 cm of a 45 cm total penetration.

q: 7. The safe bearing capacity of the soil can be improved by ...........
options: draining the soil if water table is very near the base of the footing
explain: Bearing capacity can be increased by reaching stiffer strata (depth), filling voids (grouting), or removing pore water pressure (drainage).

q: 8. In a static penetrometer test the angle of the penetrating cone is ..........
explain: The standard cone used in static (Dutch) cone penetration tests has a base area of 10 cm² and an apex angle of 60°.

q: 9. Soil investigation at a site are carried out to obtain the information regarding .........
options: the engineering and the physical properties of the soils
the details of the soil profile to considerable depth
the depth to ground water table and its seasonal fluctuations
explain: Comprehensive soil reports must include soil classification (properties), the sequence of layers (profile), and hydrological data (water table).

q: 10. In the case of soil investigation by boring, the record of soil samples arranged according the depth where they are found is known as .........
explain: A bore-log is a technical record that provides a detailed description of the soil layers encountered at various depths during a boring operation.

q: 11. The plate loading test gives .........
options: the ultimate bearing capacity of the soil
safe bearing capacity of the soil
explain: The plate load test is used to determine the ultimate bearing capacity of soil at a specific depth and to estimate the likely settlement under a given load.

q: 12. The relationship between the ultimate bearing capacity (qu), the net ultimate bearing capacity (qnu) and the depth of footing D (r being the unit weight of the soil) is:
explain: Ultimate bearing capacity (qu) is the sum of the net ultimate bearing capacity (qnu) and the overburden pressure (γD or rD).

q: 13. According to Rankine's theory, the minimum depth of foundation is given by .........
explain: Rankine's formula for minimum depth ensures the soil won't heave around the foundation; it uses the ratio of vertical to horizontal pressure squared.

q: 14. The minimum depth of foundation below the ground level in any soil is .........
explain: In general practice and to avoid frost action or surface disturbances, the minimum recommended depth for any foundation is 80 cm to 90 cm.

q: 15. The method of protecting the foundations in loose soils from caving in, is called
explain: Both timbering (planking and strutting) and shoring are used to provide temporary support to the sides of excavations in unstable soil.

q: 16. The portion of the brick obtained by cutting into two portions longitudinally is called ..........
explain: A queen closer is a brick cut in half along its length, resulting in a piece that is the full length and height but half the width of a standard brick.

q: 17. Osmosis is .........
options: an electrical process where fine grained cohesive soils are drained using electricity
a method to determine the depth to water table
explain: Electro-osmosis is a technique used to drain water from low-permeability soils like clay by applying a direct current between electrodes.

q: 18. The approximate bearing capacity of a sound rock without any defects may be taken as .........
explain: Hard, sound rocks like granite or limestone have very high bearing capacities, typically ranging from 300 to 350 t/m².

q: 19. Which of the following has the lowest bearing capacity?
explain: Moist or soft clay has very little internal friction and gains its strength only from cohesion, making it significantly weaker than sands or gravels.

q: 20. The type of foundation recommended for heavily loaded steel stanchions in soils with poor bearing capacity
explain: Grillage foundations are specifically designed to spread heavy concentrated loads from steel columns over a large area using layers of steel beams.

q: 21. Well foundation is also known as .........
explain: A well foundation is a type of deep foundation, often used for bridges, which is technically referred to as a caisson.

q: 22. The most commonly used deep foundation in buildings .........
explain: Pile foundations are the most common deep foundation used for building structures to transfer loads to deeper, more stable soil layers.

q: 23. If the load coming on to a pile is transferred to a suitable bearing stratum at its bottom end, then it is called .........
explain: An end-bearing pile transfers the structural load directly through its tip to a hard, incompressible layer of rock or dense gravel.

q: 24. If the load coming on to a pile is resisted by friction developed between the surface area of the pile and the surrounding material, then it is called .........
explain: Friction piles derive their carrying capacity from the skin friction (adhesion) between the pile surface and the surrounding soil.

q: 25. A pile which by itself does not carry any load but improves the bearing capacity of the soil is called .........
explain: Compaction piles are driven into loose granular soils to increase the soil's density (compactness) through vibration and displacement.

q: 26. A pile commonly used to reduce seepage and control the uplift pressures under hydraulic structure is known as .........
explain: Sheet piles are thin, interlocking plates driven into the ground to create a continuous barrier (cutoff wall) to prevent water seepage under dams or weirs.

q: 27. A pile which has an enlarged shape at the base is called .......
explain: A Franki pile (or pressure-injected foot pile) is characterized by a bulbous, enlarged base that provides high end-bearing resistance.

q: 28. A cast-in-situ concrete pile with one or more enlarged bulbs on its stem is called .........
explain: Under-reamed piles are bored cast-in-situ piles with one or more bulbs (reams) to provide better anchorage, especially in expansive soils like black cotton soil.

q: 29. The distance between the flanges of the beams in any tier of a grillage foundation should be equal to .........
options: one and half times the flange width or 30 cm whichever is less
explain: To ensure proper concrete placement and compaction between the steel beams, a spacing of 1.5 to 2 times the flange width (or roughly 30cm) is maintained.

q: 30. The maximum permissible differential settlement in the case of foundations on sandy soils is generally about ..........
explain: For isolated foundations on sand, the allowable differential settlement is restricted to 25 mm to prevent structural cracking.

q: 31. The maximum permissible differential settlement in the case of foundations on clayey soils is generally about ...........
explain: Clayey soils allow for a higher differential settlement (40 mm) because the settlement process is slower and more uniform over time compared to sand.

q: 32. The maximum permissible total settlement in the case of raft foundations clayey soils is generally about ...........
explain: Raft foundations distribute loads over a larger area; in clay, a total settlement of up to 100 mm is often considered the permissible limit.

q: 33. The maximum permissible total settlement in the case of raft foundations sandy soils is generally about ...........
explain: For rafts on sand, the allowable total settlement is usually limited to 65 mm (standard range 40–65 mm) to ensure stability.

q: 34. Uniform distribution of loads from walls on piles is achieved by connecting the group of piles supporting the structure ...........
options: by tie rods at the bottom of the piles
by tie rods at the top of the piles
isolating the piles without any connection
explain: A pile cap (often in the form of a reinforced concrete beam) is used to tie the piles together and distribute the wall load evenly among them.

q: 35. The offsets in the stepped strip footing in brick masonry is ..........
explain: In standard brick masonry footings, the horizontal offset for each step is typically half a brick length (approx. 5 cm to 10 cm, with 5 cm being the minimum for stability).

q: 36. The maximum permissible eccentricity of load on a rectangular foundation with width B is equal to ---
explain: According to the 'Middle Third Rule,' to avoid tension in the base of a foundation, the eccentricity (e) must not exceed B/6.

q: 37. A foundation could fail due to ..........
options: unequal distribution of weight of the structure
horizontal movement of earth adjoining the structure
explain: Foundations fail when the soil's bearing capacity is exceeded, when the soil moves laterally, or when differential settlement creates internal stresses.

q: 38. The advantage of timber piles is that they are ...........
explain: Timber piles are easy to handle (light) and can withstand driving stresses better than brittle materials, though they are prone to decay if not fully submerged.

q: 39. The safe bearing capacity under dynamic loads such as machine foundations is taken to be...
options: more than that for static loads
same as that for static loads
less than that for static loads
depends on the weight of machine
explain: Dynamic/vibratory loads can cause soil liquefaction or additional settlement, so the allowable bearing capacity is reduced (often by 25-50%) compared to static loads.

q: 40. To improve the bearing capacity of the foundation, the cement grouting may be used if the foundation consists of .........
explain: Cement grouting is effective in rocks or coarse gravels where the grout can flow into fissures and voids to create a monolithic, stronger mass.

q: 41. If the soil is water logged, its bearing capacity may be improved by .........
explain: Water logging increases pore water pressure and reduces effective stress; removing the water through drainage significantly restores soil strength.

q: 42. When two or more individual column footings are joined by a beam, it is called ........
explain: A strap footing consists of two isolated footings connected by a rigid 'strap' beam to transfer the eccentric load of one footing to the other.

q: 43. A footing which supports two columns is known as .........
explain: A combined footing is a single foundation slab that carries the load of two or more columns, usually used when columns are close together.

q: 44. If footing supports more than two columns, it is called .........
explain: A continuous footing supports a long wall or a row of three or more columns in a line.

q: 45. The safe bearing capacity of medium clay which can be readily intended with a thumb nail is taken as ............
explain: Soil consistency can be field-tested by hand; medium clay, which is moderately firm, typically has a bearing capacity around 25 t/m².

q: 46. The thickness of staining in well foundations is generally about (where D is the diameter of the well)
explain: Staining (the wall of the well) must be thick enough to resist external earth/water pressure; D/4 is a common empirical ratio for design.

q: 47. The tilt in the well foundations should not exceed .........
explain: During the sinking of caissons/wells, the vertical alignment (tilt) is strictly monitored and should not deviate more than 1 in 200.

q: 48. The piles used in the construction of coffer dams .........
explain: Coffer dams are temporary water-tight structures; sheet piles are used to create the walls that hold back the water.

q: 49. The pile used to resist large horizontal or inclined force is ...........
explain: Batten (or Batter) piles are driven at an angle (inclined) to resist lateral forces from wind, water, or earth pressure.

q: 50. The exterior corner of wall is known as ...........
explain: In masonry, the external corner of a building or the stones/bricks forming that corner are called quoins.

q: 51. The surface of the wall exposed to weather is called ...........
explain: In masonry, the 'face' is the exterior surface of a wall that is visible and exposed to the weather, while the 'back' is the inner surface.

q: 52. The portion of the wall between the facing and backing of the wall is called ...........
explain: The interior portion of a thick wall, situated between the external facing and internal backing, is filled with 'hearting' (usually rubble or lower-grade brick).

q: 53. The portion of the brick obtained by cutting into two portions longitudinally is called ...........
explain: A queen closer is a brick cut in half along its length. It is used to maintain the bond at the end of a wall (the quoin).

q: 54. The portion of the brick obtained by cutting it in transverse direction is called ...........
explain: A 'bat' is a piece of brick cut across its width. Common types include half-bats or three-quarter bats.

q: 55. The portion of a brick which is cut at one corner such that at one end its width is half of that of a full brick is called ...........
explain: A king closer is formed by cutting off a triangular piece from one corner, reaching from the middle of the header to the middle of the stretcher.

q: 56. The brick which is cut such that at one end half the width is maintained and at the other end full width is maintained is called ...........
explain: A beveled closer has one full-length stretcher face, but the width at one end is cut to be half the width of the brick.

q: 57. The brick which is cut such that no longer face is full and the other longer face is small in length is called ...........
explain: A mitred closer is cut at an angle (usually 45 to 60 degrees) along its length, so one stretcher face is shorter than the other.

q: 58. The overlapping of bricks or stones in masonry is called ...........
explain: Bonding is the arrangement of bricks or stones to ensure they overlap, preventing continuous vertical joints and distributing loads throughout the wall.

q: 59. A groove provided on the underside of projecting elements such as cornices, copings such that rain water can be discharged clear of the wall surface is called ...........
explain: Throating is a small groove on the underside of a sill or coping that prevents rainwater from running back onto the wall, protecting it from dampness.

q: 60. A brick or stone put in position in the masonry such that its length is perpendicular to the face of the wall is known as ...........
explain: A header is a brick laid so that only its smallest face (end) is visible on the surface of the wall.

q: 61. A brick or stone put in position in the masonry such that its length is parallel to the face of the wall is known as ...........
explain: A stretcher is a brick laid with its longest side (length) parallel to the face of the wall.

q: 62. In random rubble masonry ...........
options: the stones are neatly dressed and laid in courses
the stones are neatly dressed but not built to courses
the stone are either not dressed or roughly dressed and may be coursed or uncoursed
the stones are not dressed and are laid without mortar
explain: Random rubble masonry uses stones of irregular shapes and sizes, which are roughly dressed or not dressed at all, and can be laid in layers (coursed) or at random.

q: 63. The safe compressive strength of ashlar masonry of granite stone in 1:6 cement mortar may be taken as ...........
explain: Ashlar masonry uses finely dressed stones. Granite is a very hard rock, and in 1:6 cement mortar, it can safely support 160 t/m².

q: 64. A low height wall constructed along edge of the roof is called ...........
explain: A parapet wall is a low wall built at the edge of a roof or balcony for safety and to hide the roof surface.

q: 65. The tool used by the masons to check the verticality of walls is ...........
explain: A plumb bob is a weighted string used to determine a perfectly vertical line (plumb) for brickwork or stone walls.

q: 66. The vertical sides of openings for doors and window are called ...........
explain: Jambs are the vertical sides of a wall opening for a window or door, which support the lintel or arch above.

q: 67. The horizontal member spanning the window and door openings in the masonry walls is called ...........
explain: A lintel is a horizontal structural beam that spans the opening of a window or door to carry the weight of the wall above it.

q: 68. The bricks arranged projecting in alternate courses for the purpose of bonding future masonry work is called ...........
explain: Toothing is the process of leaving bricks projecting from a wall so that another wall can be bonded into it later.

q: 69. A projected stone in masonry wall provided to serve as a support to joist or truss is known as ...
explain: A corbel is a stone or brick projecting from a wall to support a heavy load, such as a beam, joist, or truss.

q: 70. A projected ornamental course near the top of the wall or near the junction of the wall and ceiling is known as ...
explain: A cornice is a decorative horizontal molding that crowns a building or furniture element, typically found at the top of a wall.

q: 71. The covering on the exposed top of a wall is called ...........
explain: Coping is a protective cap or cover (usually stone or brick) on the top of a wall to shed water and prevent moisture from entering the wall.

q: 72. A brick which has one or two rounded edges and used to obtain rounded corners in the wall is called .......
explain: A bull nose brick is manufactured with one or more rounded edges, used for aesthetics or to prevent sharp corners on walls.

q: 73. Stretcher bond is possible only in ...........
explain: Since stretcher bond only shows the long face of the brick, it can only be used for walls that are half-a-brick thick (partition walls).

q: 74. The bond which consists of alternate courses of headers and stretchers is known as ..........
explain: English bond is considered the strongest bond, consisting of one course of headers followed by one course of stretchers.

q: 75. The bond in which each course consists of alternate stretchers and headers is known as ..........
explain: In Flemish bond, headers and stretchers alternate within every single course, giving it a more decorative appearance than English bond.

q: 76. The bond in which the bonding bricks are at an inclination to the direction of the wall is known as...
explain: Raking bonds (like herring-bone or diagonal bond) place bricks at an angle to the wall's face to improve longitudinal strength.

q: 77. The English bond in which the corners of the wall are strengthened by starting every stretcher course with a three fourth bat at the quoin and a header is placed next to the three fourth bat at the quoin in alternate stretcher course is called ..........
explain: Dutch bond is a variation of English bond that uses a specific arrangement of bats and headers at the quoin to improve appearance and strength.

q: 78. The English bond in which queen closers are placed next to quoin headers and a header is introduced next to the quoin stretcher in every alternate stretcher course ..........
explain: English cross bond is similar to English bond but staggers the stretcher courses by introducing an extra header at the quoin, creating a distinctive pattern.

q: 79. A bond in which a header course is provided only after few stretcher courses is known as ..........
explain: Garden wall bond is used for thin walls; it usually consists of one course of headers for every three or five courses of stretchers.

q: 80. A junction at which two walls meet at an angle other than 90° is called ..........
explain: A squint quoin or squint junction occurs when walls meet at an angle that is not a right angle (90°).

q: 81. A tool used by masons both for lifting and spreading mortar and also to cut the bricks is ..........
explain: The trowel is the primary tool for masonry, used for handling mortar and sometimes for roughly trimming bricks.

q: 82. The steps provided in the form of brick masonry outside the door in external walls is called ..........
explain: The threshold is the brick or stone area at the base of an exterior door, often built as a low step.

q: 83. A brick masonry could fail due to ..........
options: rupture along a vertical joint in poorly bonded walls
explain: Brick walls can fail through crushing under heavy loads, sliding (shearing) between bricks, or splitting along vertical joints (rupture).

q: 84. Good bonding in the brick masonry is ensured when ..........
options: all bricks used are of uniform size
the vertical joints in alternate courses are in plumb from top to base
bats are used as sparingly as possible
explain: Strength in masonry comes from uniform materials, vertical alignment of joints (plumb), and minimizing the use of broken bricks (bats).

q: 85. A bonding in which all courses are laid as stretchers is known as ..........
explain: Stretcher bond (or running bond) is composed entirely of stretchers and is only used for thin walls.

q: 86. A bond in which stretcher bricks are laid on edge in alternate courses forming continuous cavity is known as ..........
explain: Soldier bond involves bricks laid vertically on their ends (on edge), often used for decorative purposes or window sills.

q: 87. A temporary structure erected with a purpose of providing a safe working platform is known as .......
explain: Scaffolding is the temporary framework used by workers to reach high sections of a building during construction or repair.

q: 88. An arrangement for supporting an unsafe structure temporarily, till it is rendered safe or dismantled, is known as ..........
explain: Shoring is the use of temporary supports (shores) to stabilize a building that is in danger of collapsing or undergoing renovation.

q: 89. An arrangement supporting an existing structure by providing supports underneath is known as ........
explain: Underpinning is the process of strengthening or deepening the foundation of an existing building by adding supports underneath.

q: 90. The indentation marks made on the top of the brick to provide key for holding the mortar is known as ..........
explain: The frog is the indentation on the top of a brick. It reduces weight and creates a mechanical 'key' for the mortar to bond.

q: 91. The compressive strength of first class and second class bricks should not be less than ..........
explain: Indian Standards typically specify that first-class bricks should have a minimum compressive strength of 105 kg/cm², but commonly 80-100 kg/cm² is cited as the safe minimum for structural work.

q: 92. The pressure due to wind of velocity V is proportional to ..........
explain: Wind pressure (P) follows the formula P = 0.6V², where P is in N/m² and V is wind speed in m/s; thus, it is proportional to the square of velocity.

q: 93. When two walls separated by a small gap, are connected together by metal pins, it is called .......
explain: A cavity wall consists of two leaves of masonry separated by an air space (cavity) and connected by metal wall ties.

q: 94. Cavity walls ..........
options: prevent dampness from entering the building
have lesser dead load for given wall thickness
are better insulated against heat and sound
explain: The air gap in cavity walls prevents moisture transfer (dampness) and acts as an insulator for heat and noise.

q: 95. A wall which is constructed to divide the space within the building into rooms is called ..........
explain: Partition walls are non-load-bearing internal walls used to create separate rooms within a structure.

q: 96. A load bearing partition wall is called ..........
explain: While many partitions are non-load-bearing, if an internal wall carries structural weight, it is referred to as an internal load-bearing wall.

q: 97. Brick masonry constructed within a framework of wooden member to act as a partition wall is called ..........
explain: Brick nogging is a type of wall construction where bricks are used to fill the spaces between timber studs in a wood frame.

q: 98. When first class bricks are immersed in water for one hour, the weight of water absorbed by them should not exceed ..........
explain: First-class bricks should not absorb more than 1/6th (approx. 15-20%) of their dry weight in water after 24 hours of immersion.

q: 99. A flooring which is made of thin laminated stone slabs of regular geometric shape laid on concrete bedding is called ..........
explain: Flagstone flooring consists of flat, thin stone slabs (flags) bedded in mortar over a concrete base.

q: 100. Cork flooring is essentially used in ..........
options: buildings such as libraries, theatres and broadcasting stations which are to be noiseless
explain: Cork is highly resilient and sound-absorbent, making it ideal for quiet environments like libraries or recording studios.
